bimatoprost.summary: Prescription eyelash-growth drop (Latisse) that gives longer, thicker, darker lashes for a more defined eye area, and is sometimes used on brows.

quick.overview:
Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin analogue approved as Latisse for eyelash hypotrichosis. It gives longer, thicker, darker lashes, which frames the eyes and makes the eye area look more defined. Some people also use it on eyebrows.

It is thought to prolong the growth phase of lash follicles, increase the number of follicles growing at once, and darken lashes through pigment production. Randomised trials report increases in lash length, thickness and darkness over vehicle. It was first approved as eye drops for glaucoma and received its lash approval in 2008 after patients noticed longer, darker lashes.
quick.how: It is applied along the upper lash line as a prescription solution, usually as a nightly routine, with careful application at the lash line. Lash changes build over weeks of regular use, and lashes return to baseline after people stop. Eyebrow use is off-label and based on small studies and user reports.
quick.risks: Common effects are eye redness, itching and darkening of the eyelid skin. It can cause permanent darkening of the iris, particularly in hazel or mixed-colour eyes, and periorbital fat loss that gives a sunken look. It is prescription-only in the United States; over-the-counter lash serums are regulated as cosmetics, not drugs.

angle.text: Bimatoprost is used to get longer, fuller, darker lashes, sometimes on brows too, for a more defined eye area. It prolongs the lash growth phase so more and longer lashes grow in. Lash growth is well studied; iris colour change and periorbital fat loss are known side effects.

pyrilutamide.summary: Topical androgen-receptor blocker developed for pattern hair loss, used as a local alternative to oral DHT blockers to keep scalp hair.

quick.overview:
Pyrilutamide (KX-826) is a topical, non-steroidal androgen receptor blocker developed for androgenetic alopecia and acne. People use it hoping to hold onto or thicken scalp hair with an effect that stays in the scalp rather than the whole body.

It competes with DHT for the androgen receptor in follicles, blocking the signalling that drives miniaturisation, and is metabolised quickly if absorbed. Early trials in China showed signals of benefit; a later phase 3 trial in Chinese men met its endpoint versus baseline but not versus placebo. Cosmetic formulations launched in China in 2024.
quick.how: It is applied to the scalp as a topical solution, usually daily and often alongside other hair-loss routines. Hair changes in trials were assessed over months. Users in hair-loss forums group it with RU58841 as an experimental topical anti-androgen.
quick.risks: Adverse events reported in trials were mild and mostly local, and long-term data are limited. It is investigational and not approved by a major regulator, so products obtained outside regulated channels vary in quality.

angle.text: Pyrilutamide is a topical androgen receptor blocker that users see as a scalp-only alternative to oral DHT blockers. By blocking androgen signalling in the follicle it aims to reduce miniaturisation and keep or regrow scalp hair. Phase 3 results have been mixed and it is not yet approved.

ru58841.summary: Topical antiandrogen used by hair-loss communities as a scalp-only alternative to finasteride, to slow miniaturisation and keep hair.

quick.overview:
RU58841 is a non-steroidal topical antiandrogen originally developed by Roussel Uclaf and later investigated for acne, pattern hair loss and excess hair growth. Hair-loss communities use it hoping to protect scalp hair without the side effects of oral DHT blockers.

It binds the androgen receptor and blocks DHT from activating it in scalp follicles, intended to act locally. The published research is cell, rodent, macaque and xenograft work from the 1990s, including the stumptail macaque; no controlled human trial on hair is known. Success reports come mainly from forum posts.
quick.how: Users apply it to the scalp as a solution, typically daily, as an alternative or add-on to finasteride or dutasteride. It is sold as a research chemical, often in alcohol-based liquids.
quick.risks: Human toxicity, systemic absorption and long-term effects are not established. It was never approved, and vendor products vary in purity. Alcohol-based solutions can irritate the scalp.

angle.text: RU58841 is a topical antiandrogen used by people hoping to treat hair loss without oral drug side effects. It blocks the androgen receptor in the scalp follicle, aiming to reduce miniaturisation and keep hair. Published work is animal and cell research, and success reports come mainly from forums.

biotin.summary: Common B-vitamin supplement taken for fuller hair and stronger nails; clearly helps when you are low on it.

quick.overview:
Biotin (vitamin B7) is a B vitamin widely sold as a supplement for hair, skin and nails, and some users take it for beard and lash growth. The payoff people want is fuller hair and stronger nails.

It is a cofactor for enzymes in fatty acid, glucose and amino acid metabolism, and a true deficiency causes hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial rash, which reverses when corrected. In people with normal intake, a 2017 review found 18 case reports of benefit, all in people with an underlying cause, and a 2024 review found three eligible studies, with the best placebo-controlled trial showing no difference from placebo.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily capsule, tablet or gummy, alone or in hair-skin-nails multivitamins, commonly in 1 to 10 mg products. Hair and nail changes are judged over several months. It is also found in organ meats and egg yolks.
quick.risks: Biotin is generally well tolerated, but high doses can interfere with blood tests that use biotin-streptavidin technology, including thyroid and troponin tests, giving falsely high or low results. The FDA has warned about this, and anyone having blood tests is advised to tell their clinician they take it.

angle.text: Biotin is taken for fuller hair, stronger nails and beard or lash growth. It supports the metabolism of hair and nail tissue, and correcting a deficiency restores normal hair growth. Trials in people with normal intake are limited, and high doses can distort some lab tests.

saw-palmetto.summary: Botanical DHT blocker taken as a natural alternative to finasteride to slow male pattern hair loss.

quick.overview:
Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) berry extract is among the most common natural products taken to slow male pattern hair loss, often as an alternative to finasteride. The goal is to keep more scalp hair by lowering DHT activity.

Extracts contain fatty acids and phytosterols that weakly inhibit 5-alpha-reductase in laboratory studies. A 2020 systematic review identified five randomised trials and two cohort studies reporting positive effects of oral and topical saw palmetto-containing supplements, while noting that high-quality data are lacking. Its main studied use is prostate symptoms, and effects on hair appear smaller than finasteride's.
quick.how: It is taken as an oral capsule or softgel, sometimes combined with other hair supplements, and some products are topical. Hair outcomes in trials were measured over months.
quick.risks: It is usually well tolerated, with mild stomach upset, headache and occasional effects on hormone-sensitive conditions. It may interact with anticoagulants and hormonal medications and is not recommended in pregnancy. Supplement potency varies between products.

angle.text: Saw palmetto is taken as a natural DHT blocker to slow male pattern hair loss. It weakly inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, which aims to cut follicle miniaturisation and slow hair loss. Small studies exist for hair, with smaller effects than finasteride; its main studied use is prostate symptoms.

pumpkin-seed-oil.summary: Oil taken or applied for thicker scalp hair in male pattern hair loss, with small trials reporting higher hair counts.

quick.overview:
Pumpkin seed oil, pressed from Cucurbita pepo seeds, is taken as an oral supplement or applied to the scalp by people hoping to slow or reverse male pattern hair loss and get thicker hair.

It is rich in unsaturated fatty acids, phytosterols and tocopherols, and phytosterols may weakly inhibit 5-alpha-reductase in laboratory studies. A 2014 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in men with androgenetic alopecia reported higher hair counts after 24 weeks, and a 2021 trial compared it with 5% minoxidil foam in women. Reviews describe these studies as small.
quick.how: It is usually taken as a daily capsule or oil, or used as a scalp product, often alongside approved treatments. Trial results were measured over about six months.
quick.risks: It is typically well tolerated, with occasional gastrointestinal upset or allergic reactions in people allergic to seeds. Product quality varies because it is sold as a food or supplement.

angle.text: Pumpkin seed oil is taken or applied for thicker scalp hair in male pattern hair loss. Its phytosterols may weakly reduce DHT activity at the follicle. A 2014 trial in men reported higher hair counts after 24 weeks, though studies are small.

collagen-peptides.summary: Supplement powder taken for smoother, more hydrated, more elastic skin, with trials reporting gains in hydration and elasticity.

quick.overview:
Collagen peptides, or hydrolysed collagen, are short amino acid chains from bovine, marine or porcine collagen, sold as powders, drinks and capsules. People take them for hydrated, smoother, firmer-looking skin and fewer wrinkles, and also for nails and joints.

Digested peptides, particularly hydroxyproline-containing ones, are absorbed and may signal fibroblasts to make more collagen and hyaluronic acid, or simply supply amino acids. Several randomised trials report better skin hydration, elasticity or wrinkles, and a 2026 meta-analysis of 19 trials found significant improvement in hydration and brightness with a modest effect on wrinkles. A 2025 meta-analysis found the benefits shrink or vanish in higher-quality, non-industry-funded trials. No hair-growth effect is reported.
quick.how: It is taken daily, mixed into drinks or smoothies or as capsules, often with vitamin C, and skin trials usually run for weeks to months.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally mild, such as bloating or an unpleasant taste, and allergy is possible with marine or bovine sources. Supplements are lightly regulated and heavy metal contamination has been flagged in some products.

angle.text: Collagen peptides are taken for hydrated, elastic, smoother-looking skin. They supply collagen-building amino acids and may signal skin cells to make more collagen. Trials report gains in hydration and elasticity, many industry-funded, and a 2025 meta-analysis found smaller effects in higher-quality trials.

melatonin-topical.summary: Melatonin solution applied to the scalp for thicker hair, based on follicle receptors and antioxidant action.

quick.overview:
Melatonin is best known as a sleep hormone, but hair follicles make it and carry melatonin receptors. Topical melatonin solutions are applied to the scalp by people hoping to slow hair loss and get thicker hair.

It is proposed to prolong the follicle growth phase and reduce oxidative stress in the scalp. A 2023 review identified 11 human studies in 2,267 patients and reported that eight observed positive outcomes in androgenetic alopecia, mainly more hair growth, density and shaft thickness versus controls. A 2024 review noted that most hair studies did not clearly demonstrate efficacy.
quick.how: It is used as a scalp solution applied regularly, usually alongside other hair-loss routines. Trials ran for a few months.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally well tolerated, with possible scalp irritation, or drowsiness if enough is absorbed. Melatonin is over the counter in the United States but prescription-only in parts of Europe, and long-term topical safety data are limited.

angle.text: Topical melatonin is applied to the scalp for thicker hair. Follicles carry melatonin receptors, and melatonin is thought to support the growth phase and reduce oxidative stress. A 2023 review found eight of 11 human studies reported positive outcomes, though most hair studies did not clearly demonstrate efficacy.

vitamin-d.summary: Vitamin that supports bone and follicle biology; correcting a low level can help deficiency-related hair loss.

quick.overview:
Vitamin D is made in the skin from UVB light and obtained from oily fish, fortified foods and supplements. People take it for hair, bone health, hormones and sleep, with the appearance payoff being less hair loss when levels are low.

Calcitriol, its active form, binds the vitamin D receptor in follicle keratinocytes, which is needed for normal follicle cycling. Low blood levels have been reported in telogen effluvium and alopecia areata, and deficiency is diagnosed with a blood test. Whether supplementing people with normal levels changes hair outcomes has not been established by trials.
quick.how: It is taken as an over-the-counter daily supplement, often alongside calcium and K2, and sun exposure also raises levels. People commonly check their level with a blood test first.
quick.risks: Excess supplementation can cause hypercalcaemia, kidney stones and kidney damage, mostly with very high doses over long periods. The large VITAL trial found no reduction in invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events in the general population.

angle.text: Vitamin D is taken to correct low levels linked to some hair-loss conditions and to support bone. It acts on follicle receptors involved in hair cycling, so fixing a deficiency can reduce related shedding. Studies of supplementing people with adequate levels for hair or height are lacking.

iron.summary: Essential mineral; correcting low iron stores can stop deficiency-related hair shedding.

quick.overview:
Iron is needed for oxygen transport and many enzymes. People with diffuse hair shedding, fatigue or pallor take it hoping to bring hair back to normal density, and some take it for under-eye shadows.

Follicle cells divide quickly and depend on iron-containing enzymes, and low stores are thought to push follicles early into the resting phase, causing telogen effluvium. Clinicians commonly check ferritin and haemoglobin in unexplained shedding, and correcting a confirmed deficiency is the accepted treatment for deficiency-related shedding. No randomised trial in the available research tests iron for hair outcomes.
quick.how: Oral iron is usually taken as a daily tablet after a blood test such as ferritin confirms low stores, often with vitamin C and apart from calcium. Shedding recovers over months as stores refill.
quick.risks: Oral iron commonly causes constipation, nausea and dark stools. Excess iron accumulates in people with haemochromatosis and promotes oxidative damage, and accidental overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six. Guidance advises testing first.

angle.text: Iron is supplemented by people with diffuse hair shedding or pale skin who have low iron. Follicles depend on iron-containing enzymes, so restoring low stores lets hair cycle normally and reduces shedding. Benefits with normal iron levels are untested.

teriparatide.summary: Prescription bone-building injection for osteoporosis that is discussed in bone-focused circles for jaw and facial structure.

quick.overview:
Teriparatide is a recombinant fragment of parathyroid hormone (residues 1-34) given as a daily injection for osteoporosis. In bone-focused looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a drug that builds new bone and might thicken the jaw and sharpen facial structure.

It activates the PTH1 receptor on bone-forming cells, increasing bone formation more than resorption with intermittent exposure, with the largest effect in spinal bone. Randomised trials show fewer vertebral fractures in osteoporosis patients. No published study has tested it for facial bone in healthy adults.
quick.how: Prescribed for osteoporosis as a daily injection under medical supervision, with treatment duration limits. Use for facial structure is speculation discussed in forums.
quick.risks: Effects include nausea, dizziness, leg cramps and raised blood calcium. Osteosarcoma appeared in high-dose rodent studies, which led to a former boxed warning and duration limits. It is prescription-only, costly, and its approvals cover osteoporosis only.

angle.text: In bone-focused circles teriparatide is discussed as a way to thicken facial bone and sharpen the jaw. It stimulates new bone formation in osteoporosis patients, and the idea is that this could carry over to the face. No study has tested facial bone change in healthy adults.

romosozumab.summary: Sclerostin-blocking osteoporosis antibody that builds bone, mentioned in bone-focused circles for facial structure.

quick.overview:
Romosozumab (Evenity) is an antibody given as a monthly injection for up to 12 months to treat osteoporosis in people at high fracture risk. Bone-focused users mention it as another bone builder that could in theory change jaw and facial structure.

It binds sclerostin, a protein from bone osteocytes that restrains bone formation, which raises formation and reduces resorption and increases bone density quickly, especially in spine and hip. Phase 3 trials found large reductions in vertebral fractures. No study has examined facial or skeletal structure in healthy people.
quick.how: It is prescribed for osteoporosis and given by clinicians as a monthly injection for up to a year, usually followed by another bone drug. Use for appearance is theoretical.
quick.risks: It carries a boxed warning for heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death. Other concerns include low blood calcium, injection-site reactions, and rare osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures. It is a prescription drug approved only for osteoporosis.

angle.text: Romosozumab is mentioned by bone-focused users as a bone builder that might change jaw and facial structure. It blocks sclerostin, which raises bone formation and density in osteoporosis patients. Facial effects in healthy people have not been studied.

vitamin-k2.summary: Fat-soluble vitamin taken in bone and facial-structure stacks to help calcium go into bone and keep arteries clear.

quick.overview:
Vitamin K2 (menaquinones, mainly MK-4 and MK-7) is found in natto, some cheeses and animal products, and is commonly taken with vitamin D3 and calcium in bone and facial-structure stacks. People take it hoping for firmer bone and structure.

It is a cofactor for the enzyme that activates osteocalcin, which helps bind calcium into bone, and matrix Gla protein, which limits soft-tissue calcification. A 2022 meta-analysis in postmenopausal women found improved lumbar-spine density but no significant difference in fractures. No study has tested it for facial bone in healthy adults.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily capsule, often combined with D3, calcium and magnesium. MK-7 stays in circulation longer than MK-4.
quick.risks: Supplements are generally well tolerated and no upper limit has been set. Vitamin K interacts with warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, so people on anticoagulants need medical advice.

angle.text: Vitamin K2 is taken alongside D3 and calcium for bone, facial structure and height. It activates the proteins that bind calcium into bone matrix. Trials look at bone density and arterial calcification; facial or height effects in healthy adults are anecdotal.

calcium.summary: Raw mineral for bone; adequate intake supports bone density and peak bone mass, mainly when diet falls short.

quick.overview:
Calcium is the main mineral in bones and teeth. People pair it with D3 and K2 aiming at bone density, height potential or facial structure, and it comes from dairy, fortified foods, leafy greens and supplements.

It is deposited as hydroxyapatite in bone matrix, and adequate intake supports mineralisation and peak bone mass. Meta-analyses report small increases in bone density from higher intake, while evidence that calcium or vitamin D prevents fractures in older adults is mixed. No study has tested calcium for changing facial or jaw bone in healthy adults.
quick.how: It comes from food or a daily supplement, often combined with vitamin D, K2 and magnesium. Supplements help mainly when dietary intake is low.
quick.risks: Excess supplements can cause constipation, kidney stones and hypercalcaemia, and some studies raise questions about cardiovascular effects of high-dose supplements. It can interact with certain antibiotics and thyroid medicines.

angle.text: Calcium is the raw mineral for bone, taken with D3 and K2 by people aiming at bone density, height potential or facial structure. It supports bone mass and mineralisation when intake would otherwise be low. Appearance effects such as height gain or facial change are untested.

magnesium.summary: Mineral taken for better sleep, recovery and muscle relaxation, which supports less puffiness, better skin and training.

quick.overview:
Magnesium is an essential mineral used in hundreds of enzyme reactions and held about half in bone. Looksmaxxers take it for sleep quality, cramps and recovery, with the payoff of better rest, less puffiness, and better training and skin; some apply magnesium oil to the scalp.

It supports nerve and muscle function and energy production. Evidence is strongest for correcting a deficiency; for sleep, trials report mixed findings, with one meta-analysis in older adults finding shorter time to fall asleep. No study has tested it for facial structure.
quick.how: It is usually taken as an evening supplement or from nuts, seeds, legumes and greens. Common forms include citrate, glycinate and oxide.
quick.risks: Supplements commonly cause loose stools and abdominal cramping, and people with kidney impairment can accumulate dangerous levels. It can interact with some antibiotics and bisphosphonates.

angle.text: Magnesium is taken for deeper sleep, relaxation and recovery, which can mean less puffiness, better skin and better training. It supports muscle relaxation and sleep. Evidence for sleep is modest and mixed; hair and appearance uses rest mostly on user reports.

boron.summary: Trace element taken in the belief that it raises free testosterone for a leaner, more masculine look, and for bone and joints.

quick.overview:
Boron is a trace element from fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes, sold as boric acid, calcium fructoborate or boron citrate. In appearance circles it is taken in the belief that it raises free testosterone and lowers SHBG, supporting a more masculine physique, and for bone and joint health.

It is proposed to influence calcium, magnesium and vitamin D metabolism and sex-hormone levels. A 2008 review found little systematic study of its effects in humans, while a 2015 review argues it matters for bone, wound healing, hormones and vitamin D use. Hormone and bone studies in people are small.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily supplement, often within testosterone-support or bone stacks, in addition to dietary sources.
quick.risks: Food intake is safe, but high supplemental doses can cause nausea, diarrhoea and toxicity, and an upper intake level has been set. Reviews describe fatalities from boric acid ingestion and reproductive toxicity in animals; it is advised to avoid in pregnancy without medical advice.

angle.text: Boron is taken in the belief that it raises free testosterone and lowers SHBG, supporting muscle and a more masculine look, plus bone and joint health. It is proposed to act on hormone and mineral metabolism. Small human studies exist on hormones and bone; appearance effects are untested.

bpc-157.summary: Healing peptide used by lifters to recover from tendon and muscle injuries so training stays consistent; research is mainly animal.

quick.overview:
BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide modelled on a protein fragment from human gastric juice. Lifters use it hoping to heal tendons, ligaments, muscle and gut faster, so they can keep training and build physique.

Preclinical work suggests it may influence angiogenesis, growth-hormone receptor expression in tendon fibroblasts and nitric oxide pathways, which could speed cell migration and repair. The literature is overwhelmingly rodent studies, largely from one research group, and a 2025 systematic review found almost no human clinical data.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide or through compounding channels and is often stacked with TB-500 in recovery routines. People use it around injuries for weeks.
quick.risks: Human safety data are minimal, so the risk profile is largely unknown. Concerns include product purity and identity, injection-site problems, and a theoretical concern that pro-angiogenic activity could matter for people with cancer risk. It has no approved medical use, US regulators have flagged evidence and safety gaps, and WADA prohibits it for tested athletes.

angle.text: BPC-157 is used by lifters who want faster healing of tendons and muscles so injuries cost less training time. Quicker repair means more consistent training and more muscle. Nearly all evidence is from animal studies, with very limited human data.

tb-500.summary: Research peptide stacked with BPC-157 for faster soft-tissue recovery; what vendors sell under the name varies.

quick.overview:
TB-500 is the name research-peptide vendors use for a synthetic version of thymosin beta-4, or a fragment of it. Lifters use it, often with BPC-157, for faster recovery of muscle and tendon injuries, and some claim skin and anti-ageing benefits.

Thymosin beta-4 binds actin and in animal models has been linked to angiogenesis, lower inflammation and better cell survival in injured tissue. Research on the full protein concerns wound, corneal and cardiac repair. Analysis of a veterinary TB-500 product found a short fragment (residues 17 to 23) rather than the full protein, and human evidence for the fragment is scarce.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide and used in recovery stacks around injuries. What is in a given vial can differ by vendor.
quick.risks: Human safety data are lacking and product identity and purity are inconsistent. Pro-angiogenic activity is a theoretical concern in people with cancer risk. It is not an approved drug and thymosin beta-4 is prohibited by WADA.

angle.text: TB-500 is used, often with BPC-157, by lifters who want faster recovery from muscle and tendon injuries, and some claim skin and anti-ageing benefits. Quicker repair means more consistent training. Evidence is preclinical, and what vendors sell under the name varies.

kpv.summary: Short anti-inflammatory peptide from alpha-MSH, promoted for calmer, less irritated skin and gut without tanning.

quick.overview:
KPV is a three-amino-acid peptide (lysine-proline-valine) from the end of alpha-MSH. It keeps the hormone's anti-inflammatory activity without the pigmentation effect, and people use it hoping for calmer skin, gut healing and soft-tissue recovery.

In preclinical studies it enters inflamed intestinal cells through the PepT1 transporter and dampens NF-kB and MAPK signalling, lowering inflammatory cytokines. The research is cell and mouse work, particularly colitis models, and no completed human trial for appearance or recovery was identified.
quick.how: It is sold as a research peptide and often bundled with BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu in peptide stacks.
quick.risks: Human safety and efficacy data are lacking. Vendor products are unregulated with variable purity and stability, and KPV is not an approved drug. Self-injecting or ingesting unregulated peptides carries contamination and unknown-effect risks.

angle.text: KPV is used by people hoping for calmer, clearer, less irritated skin and a settled gut without the tanning effect of full alpha-MSH. It dampens inflammation signalling in cells. Evidence is from cell and mouse studies, with no completed human trial for appearance.

thymosin-alpha-1.summary: Immune-modulating peptide used in peptide stacks, with some users hoping for a healthier, younger look; human research covers medical conditions.

quick.overview:
Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid peptide first isolated from thymus tissue. Its synthetic form, thymalfasin, is approved in some countries for hepatitis B and C. In biohacking circles it is used as an immune optimiser, and some users claim a healthier look or slower visible ageing.

It is thought to act on Toll-like receptors on dendritic cells, promoting T-cell maturation and stronger immune responses. Its human research covers chronic viral hepatitis, sepsis, severe infections and cancer adjunct care, not appearance. A 2025 review argues its immune effects may be relevant to age-related immune decline.
quick.how: In clinical settings it is prescribed in some countries for specific diseases. In biohacking circles it appears in peptide stacks used by people who already use other peptides.
quick.risks: In clinical studies it is generally well tolerated, with mild injection-site reactions most common, though trial quality and safety reporting vary. Immune stimulation is a concern in autoimmune disease or transplant settings. It is not approved by the US FDA, and gray-market products are unregulated.

angle.text: Thymosin alpha-1 appears in peptide stacks as an immune booster, with some users hoping for fewer infections and a healthier, younger look. It modulates immune signalling, and human trials cover hepatitis and infections. The appearance claim has not been tested.
